This document explains the regression tree and the MARS model for life
satisfaction (`stflife`, 0--10) in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania (ESS rounds
9--11). The models are fitted in `scripts/04_tree_mars.R`, which also saves
the figures, the test metrics and the test predictions used in the group
comparison. Fitting MARS takes about 10 minutes, so this document does not fit
the models again: the fitting code is shown, and the results are read from the
saved models in `data/tree_mars_models.rds`. This document does not write any
files.

To render it, run `01_clean.R`, `03_train_test_split.R` and `04_tree_mars.R`
first, then `quarto render scripts/04_tree_mars_documentation.qmd`.

# Setup

The code runs from the repository root, so the paths are the same as in the
R scripts.

```{r setup}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
```

```{r packages}
library(dplyr)
library(caret)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(earth)
```

The train and test sets come from `03_train_test_split.R`. Missing predictor
values are already filled there (median or most common category from the train
set), and the `imputed` column marks the filled rows.

```{r data}
train <- readRDS("data/ess_train.rds")
test  <- readRDS("data/ess_test.rds")
models <- readRDS("data/tree_mars_models.rds")
fit_tree <- models$tree
fit_mars <- models$mars

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
```

# Predictors and cross-validation

Both models use the same 22 predictors as the other group models, as defined in
`03_train_test_split.R`. Age is used as a number (`agea`), not in groups, so
the models can find where the effect of age changes.

```{r predictors}
predictors <- c("agea", "female", "hincfel", "activity_grp", "health", "sclmeet",
                "partner", "trstprl", "rlgdgr", "eisced", "domicil", "russian_home",
                "inprdsc", "sclact", "hhmmb", "ppltrst", "stfeco", "stfhlth",
                "aesfdrk", "ever_unemployed", "cntry", "round")
f <- reformulate(predictors, response = "stflife")
```

The tuning parameters are chosen with 10-fold cross-validation. The folds come
from the `fold` column made in `03_train_test_split.R`, so all group models are
tuned on the same folds. For each fold, the model is fitted on the other nine
folds and tested on the one left out.

```{r folds, eval = FALSE}
folds <- sort(unique(train$fold))
index <- lapply(folds, function(k) which(train$fold != k))
names(index) <- paste0("Fold", folds)
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", index = index)
```

# Regression tree

## Method

A regression tree splits people into groups with yes/no questions, one
variable at a time (for example, "is satisfaction with the economy below
4.5?"). The prediction for a person is the average life satisfaction of their
final group (terminal node). The complexity parameter `cp` controls how much
the tree is pruned: a large `cp` gives a small tree that may miss patterns, a
small `cp` gives a large tree that follows noise in the training data. The tree
is fitted with the survey weights (`anweight`).

```{r tree-fit, eval = FALSE}
fit_tree <- train(f, data = train,
                  method = "rpart",
                  weights = train$anweight,
                  tuneLength = 20,
                  trControl = ctrl)
```

## Results

```{r tree-cv}
fit_tree$bestTune
fit_tree$results[rownames(fit_tree$bestTune), c("cp", "RMSE", "Rsquared", "MAE")]
```

```{r tree-cv-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(fit_tree)
```

```{r tree-plot, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 9}
rpart.plot(fit_tree$finalModel)
```

```{r tree-varimp, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(varImp(fit_tree), top = 15)
```

The regression tree was tuned with 10-fold cross-validation over the complexity
parameter (selected cp = 0.0033), which gave a tree with 14 terminal nodes. On
the test set it reached a weighted RMSE of 1.87 and R² of 0.31. The tree uses
only three variables: satisfaction with the economy, feeling about household
income and self-rated health. The first split separates people who rate the
economy below 5, and the least satisfied group (predicted 2.9) combines very
low satisfaction with the economy with great difficulty living on the current
income, while the most satisfied group (predicted 8.5) rates the economy at 8
or higher and lives comfortably or copes on its income. Country and age were
not used in any split. A slightly larger tree (cp = 0.002, 22 terminal nodes)
had almost the same cross-validation error and also used age, main activity and
trust, but larger trees predicted worse. The strong role of satisfaction with
the economy should be interpreted with caution, as it may partly reflect a
general tendency to answer positively.

# MARS

## Method

MARS (Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines) is a linear regression whose
lines may bend. It builds the model from hinge functions such as
`h(agea - 68) = max(0, agea - 68)`, which is 0 up to age 68 and then grows by
one per year. The bend points (knots) are found from the data. The model is
built in two steps: a forward pass adds the hinge terms that reduce the error
most, and a backward pass removes the least useful ones.

Two tuning parameters are chosen by cross-validation:

- `degree`: 1 means no interactions, 2 means two variables may be multiplied.
- `nprune`: the largest number of terms kept after the backward pass (2--30).

Interactions are allowed only between country or ESS round and another
predictor (for example, health × Latvia). This checks whether the same factors
matter in the same way in each country and round. Products of two other
variables (for example, health × income) and country × round are not allowed.

MARS is fitted without survey weights. With weights, one fit took more than 9
minutes, so the tuning would take several hours, while without weights one fit
takes a few seconds. Country and round are predictors, and the test results are
still weighted.

```{r mars-fit, eval = FALSE}
allowed_cr <- function(degree, pred, parents, namesx, first) {
  if (degree < 2) return(TRUE)
  is_cr <- grepl("^cntry|^round", namesx)
  xor(is_cr[pred], any(is_cr[parents != 0]))
}

fit_mars <- train(f, data = train,
                  method = "earth",
                  tuneGrid = expand.grid(degree = 1:2, nprune = 2:30),
                  allowed = allowed_cr,
                  trControl = ctrl)
```

## Results

```{r mars-cv}
fit_mars$bestTune
fit_mars$results[rownames(fit_mars$bestTune), c("degree", "nprune", "RMSE", "Rsquared", "MAE")]

# best result with and without interactions
r <- fit_mars$results
do.call(rbind, lapply(split(r, r$degree), function(x) x[which.min(x$RMSE), c("degree", "nprune", "RMSE", "Rsquared")]))
```

```{r mars-cv-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(fit_mars)
```

The coefficients of the selected model. `h()` terms are the hinge functions,
and the number inside is the knot.

```{r mars-summary}
summary(fit_mars$finalModel)
```

```{r mars-varimp, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(varImp(fit_mars), top = 15)
```

The plots below show the effect of each variable, with all other variables
held at typical values.

```{r mars-effects, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 9}
plotmo(fit_mars$finalModel, caption = "")
```

MARS was tuned with 10-fold cross-validation over the number of terms (2--30)
and the degree of interaction (1 or 2), where interactions were allowed only
between country or ESS round and another predictor. Because fitting with survey
weights was computationally too slow, MARS was fitted without weights, while
the test results are weighted. The selected model has 21 terms using 16
predictors and two interactions. On the test set it reached a weighted RMSE of
1.78, MAE of 1.35 and R² of 0.38. The most important variables were
satisfaction with the economy, feeling about household income and self-rated
health. Each point of satisfaction with the economy below 5 lowers predicted
life satisfaction by 0.32, and each step from coping to finding it difficult or
very difficult to live on the current income lowers it by 0.67, as does each
step from fair to bad or very bad health (0.70). Living with a partner (+0.33)
and being female (+0.26) are associated with higher, and unemployment (−0.54)
with lower life satisfaction. Age has no effect until 68, after which predicted
satisfaction rises by 0.03 points per year. Once these factors are held
constant, Latvia is 0.32 points more satisfied than Lithuania. The two selected
interactions are small: in round 11, low satisfaction with the economy lowered
life satisfaction less than in earlier rounds, and in Estonia, being less
socially active than people of the same age mattered less. Allowing these
interactions reduced the cross-validation error only negligibly (RMSE 1.774
with and without them), which suggests that the main factors work similarly
across the three countries and rounds. The model overestimates very low and
underestimates very high satisfaction.

## Residual checks

MARS gives no p-values, so normal residuals are not needed. The residuals vs
fitted plot shows diagonal stripes because life satisfaction is a whole number
from 0 to 10; there is no strong pattern. The QQ plot shows large negative
residuals: people with very low satisfaction are predicted too high.

```{r mars-residuals, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 8}
plot(fit_mars$finalModel, caption = "")
```

# Test set

The test set is used only once, to compare the final models. All metrics are
weighted with `anweight`. MARS lines can go above 10, so MARS predictions are
cut to the 0--10 scale; the tree always stays inside it, because it predicts
group means.

```{r test}
wmetrics <- function(obs, pred, w) {
  c(RMSE     = sqrt(sum(w * (obs - pred)^2) / sum(w)),
    MAE      = sum(w * abs(obs - pred)) / sum(w),
    Rsquared = 1 - sum(w * (obs - pred)^2) /
                   sum(w * (obs - weighted.mean(obs, w))^2))
}

pred_tree <- predict(fit_tree, newdata = test)
pred_mars <- pmin(pmax(as.vector(predict(fit_mars, newdata = test)), 0), 10)

round(rbind(Tree = wmetrics(test$stflife, pred_tree, test$anweight),
            MARS = wmetrics(test$stflife, pred_mars, test$anweight)), 4)
```

Each box shows the predictions for the people who gave that answer. The red
line is a perfect prediction. Both models predict very low answers too high and
very high answers too low, which is common when the outcome is skewed towards
the upper end of the scale.

```{r obs-pred, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 9}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
boxplot(pred_tree ~ test$stflife, at = sort(unique(test$stflife)),
        xlim = c(-0.5, 10.5), ylim = c(0, 10),
        xlab = "Observed", ylab = "Predicted", main = "Tree: Obs vs Pred")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lty = 2)
boxplot(pred_mars ~ test$stflife, at = sort(unique(test$stflife)),
        xlim = c(-0.5, 10.5), ylim = c(0, 10),
        xlab = "Observed", ylab = "Predicted", main = "MARS: Obs vs Pred")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lty = 2)
```
